paragraph.text: A9. "Rights are a human invention, only for humans"

that rights are a human creation says nothing about whom they should protect. On the contrary: if we create them, extending them is our choice, and that choice needs a justification. The argument also ignores that the law already protects animals, from Article 13 of the EU Treaty to the German and Brazilian constitutions.
A. Sentience and moral status ·
DIR
1. Formulation
"Rights were invented by us, for us. Animals don't come into it."
Rights don't exist in nature: they're conventions created by human communities.
A convention holds only among the members of the community that created it.
Animals aren't part of that community and took no part in creating it.
So rights don't apply to animals.
The argument has two variants. The
one denies the existence of natural rights, in the line of Jeremy Bentham, who called natural rights "nonsense upon stilts". The
one says each society invents its own, and ours chose these.
It's close to A7, but not the same. A7 demands reciprocity; A9 appeals to origin: rights would be ours because we made them.
The argument is
. Its
fails at P2, which is false as a description of how law works, and in the general leap: a norm's origin doesn't determine its scope.

3. Answer for children

It's true that we invented the rules. But think of it this way: the rules of football were invented too, and they don't apply only to the people who invented them. If the rules are ours, we can decide whom they protect. And then the right question becomes: who can get hurt by what we do? The answer includes animals.
4. Short answer

Saying something was invented by us doesn't say whom it applies to. Mathematics was also created by humans, and numbers don't hold only among mathematicians. Besides, the argument turns against whoever uses it: if we decide whom rights apply to, then excluding animals is a choice, and choices need a justification. And real law already includes them: the EU Treaty recognizes animals as sentient beings, and several constitutions, including Germany's and Brazil's, protect them from cruelty.
"If a country abolished by law the rights of a group of people, would that make it right to treat them as things?"
5. Full answer
(a) Reconstruction and diagnosis
The argument commits the
: it judges a norm's scope by its origin. Origin and scope are independent questions, as trivial cases show.
Human creation
Whom it applies to
Mathematics
The whole universe, not just mathematicians
Veterinary medicine
Animals, though created by humans
Traffic rules
Tourists who never voted for them
Children's rights
Those who took part in no deliberation
Protection of future generations
Those who don't even exist yet

There's also a problem of self-defeat. If rights are our invention, so is their scope. The argument then says: "we decided they don't apply to animals". That isn't a reason; it's a description of the decision under discussion.
(b) Where the argument breaks

Legal conventions constantly protect those who took no part in creating them: babies, people in a coma, foreigners, future generations, historical heritage. Participation has never been a condition of protection.

text.bold: 2. The history of law is a history of extension.

paragraph.text: The abolition of slavery, women's suffrage, the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006) were each, in their time, called excessive. In all of them, the answer "it's always been this way" lost.

Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union requires member states to pay full regard to the welfare of animals "since animals are sentient beings". Germany added animals to its Basic Law in 2002. Brazil's Constitution, in Article 225, prohibits practices that "subject animals to cruelty". If rights applied only to humans, these norms would be unintelligible.

text.bold: 4. Skepticism about rights doesn't imply indifference to suffering.

paragraph.text: The man who coined "nonsense upon stilts" against natural rights was Bentham, the same author of "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?" One can doubt natural rights and still recognize duties.

text.bold: 5. Ethics doesn't depend on the word "right".

paragraph.text: A consequentialist ethics does without the language of rights: if there's avoidable suffering, there's a moral reason against causing it. Dismissing rights as fiction doesn't eliminate that reason.

If validity comes only from local convention, then where the law allowed slavery there was nothing wrong, and abolition was not a moral correction, just a change of taste. Practically no one accepts that consequence.

text.bold: 7. Being invented doesn't make ethics arbitrary.

paragraph.text: Mathematics and medicine were also created by humans, and in them there are better and worse answers. In ethics, there are positions that weigh the harms and benefits of those affected in a biased way and others that don't. From the fact that rights are a human creation it doesn't follow that we may do as we please with those who took no part in creating them. See

(d) The strongest counter-reply: rights as an institution, not a label

The sophisticated version doesn't say animal suffering doesn't matter. It says "right" is a complex institution, presupposing title, exercise, representation and practical reciprocity. Extending that institution to beings who can't exercise it would create conceptual confusion and enormous practical problems, and it would be better to protect animals through human duties and welfare standards.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: It's a thesis about the tool, not about value.

paragraph.text: Even if "right" isn't the ideal instrument, the question remains of what we owe animals.

text.bold: The problem of exercise is already solved in law.

paragraph.text: Guardianship and legal representation exist precisely for holders who can't act for themselves.

text.bold: The alternative route already exists and is violated.

paragraph.text: If protection is to come through welfare duties, industrial livestock farming breaches them at scale, as the family B chapters show.

text.bold: In practice, the reply is usually used to change nothing.

paragraph.text: Those who defend it rarely propose the alternative model of protection it promises.
Recognizing that rights are a human creation is admitting that we can and should discuss whom they apply to. That's exactly what this book does.

8. Contradictions

text.bold: Condemns rights violations in other countries.

paragraph.text: Whoever thinks torture wrong when practiced by a state that authorizes it is already admitting a moral criterion above local convention.
The same person usually thinks it right to punish someone who beats a dog, which only makes sense if protecting animals is legitimate.

text.bold: Invokes rights when they're the one harmed.

paragraph.text: No one suffering an injustice says "but after all, rights are just a convention".

text.bold: Accepts protection for those who weren't party to the agreement.

paragraph.text: Children, foreigners and future generations are protected without having invented anything.
Almost everyone considers abolition and women's suffrage moral progress, not mere changes of convention.

The principle being tested is: "rights hold only for those who invented them or those local convention recognizes".
Applied to
What would follow
Note

We'd have no duties to them. They invented nothing, take no part and can't demand anything

An octopus would have moral value in the UK and none once it crossed the border. Its capacity to suffer wouldn't change; only the convention would

11. What the argument gets right

Rights really are social constructions. They aren't written in nature, they depend on institutions to exist in practice and they need careful design: who represents the holder, which specific rights make sense, how to resolve conflicts. Those who treat rights as obvious natural facts oversimplify, and Bentham's skepticism has merit on this point.

But recognizing that we build these norms increases responsibility rather than diluting it. If the boundary was drawn by us, it can't be invoked as if it were a natural limit. It's exactly what's under discussion.
